The Arizona State Office's formal public room is located on the 8th floor of BLM Arizona's State Office. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Arizona Strip District Office and Public Lands Information Center The Arizona Strip District is the Bureau of Land Management’s northernmost district in Arizona, encompassing more than 2.7 million acres of remote public lands located north of the Grand Canyon and south of the Utah state line. The closest town to the east of the district is Page, Arizona, and the closest town to the west is Mesquite, Nevada. The public lands information center and district office are located in St. George, Utah, the largest nearby city. As one of the most rugged and least developed regions in the lower 48 states, the Arizona Strip region requires careful planning and preparation. Visitors should be ready for remote backcountry travel on unimproved roads, limited services, and potentially extreme weather conditions. The Arizona Strip District is managed for conservation, recreation, grazing, cultural resource protection, and a variety of multiple‑use activities. The district includes four management units: the Arizona Strip Field Office , Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, Grand Canyon–Parashant National Monument jointly managed under a service first agreement

Photograph: Parker Haeg/Demotix/Corbis Democrats were on track to win four seats in the state senate and at least four in the house of representatives. Photograph: Parker Haeg/Demotix/Corbis Arizona This article is more than 14 years old Arizona's 'one-pizza' Democrats taste success as GOP shares slice of the pie This article is more than 14 years old Democrats' numbers in state legislature no longer tiny enough to share just one pizza after ending Republican super-majority Rory Carroll in Los Angeles Thu 8 Nov 2012 15.58 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Arizona Democrats are the "one-pizza caucus" no more. Their numbers in the state legislature – paltry enough to share a single pizza, went the joke – have surged and ended the Republican super-majority. Democrats were on track to win four seats in the state senate and at least four in the house of representatives in the wake of Tuesday's election, eroding GOP control over one of the south's most conservative states. Democrats hailed it as a "correction" to GOP overreach. "It's a beginning we can build upon," said one blogger . The Republican advantage in the senate shrank to 17-13, giving Democrats some muscle in looming fights over Medicaid expansion and the state's much-criticised immigration laws. pages.title: Artemis IV - NASA
pages.description: NASA is targeting the first Artemis lunar landing in early 2028. After launching the crew aboard the Orion spacecraft, they will transfer to a commercial lunar lander for transport to the surface of the Moon. Lander readiness will determine which provider will safely carry them to the surface and back to Orion in lunar orbit before the crew returns home aboard Orion—splashing down safely in the Pacific Ocean.

These fossils were preserved within expanding and contracting wetlands between 100,000-12,500 years ago. Many of the Pleistocene animals of Tule Springs are still alive today, including the coyote ( Canis latrans ), jackrabbit ( Lepus sp.), and aquatic snails. Some animals went extinct, disappearing from North America entirely. Columbian mammoths belonged to the same family as living elephants. Our mission is to prevent extinction of plants and animals in the parks, and to restore species that have occurred in parks historically but have been lost due a variety of factors. The at-risk species program coordinates and collaborates with partners on actions to sustain biodiversity and ecological systems that support at-risk species. pages.text: Austrian and Swiss women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya 22 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Basillioh Rukanga and Makuochi Okafor , BBC Africa Christoph Greztmacher Eva Greztmacher, 76, had spent many years in Niger as an aid worker Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi. Austrian national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Swiss Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year. No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed. The Austrian and Swiss governments have both confirmed the release of their citizens. The Swiss government said Abbt was free and on her way back to Switzerland, while Austria said Gretzmacher had been released after "intensive diplomatic efforts". "We are all very relieved that Eva G. is free again after more than 21 months... For many months, we worked closely, discreetly, and in a spirit of trust with our regional, European, and international partners.
